**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

We've been circling this question for a few weeks now, usually in hallway conversations that end with "we should write this down properly." This memo is that attempt. The question on the table is whether we should spend roughly $180K on two additional GPU nodes, or invest the next quarter in raising utilisation on the hardware we already own, which currently sits at about 34% average occupancy with a peak of 71% during the Tuesday batch window.

Let me start with the uncomfortable observation: our instinct in this team has historically been to buy. Buying feels like progress. It's legible in a budget review, it arrives in crates, and nobody has to have a hard conversation about why the existing fleet is idle most of the day. But 34% utilisation on hardware we purchased eighteen months ago is not a capacity problem. It's a scheduling and ownership problem wearing a capacity costume, and if we buy our way out of it, we will very likely reproduce the same pattern on the new machines within two quarters.

The case for buying is real, though, and I don't want to strawman it. Our inference latency has degraded at peak: p99 response times on the customer-facing endpoint have crept from 380ms to nearly 900ms over the last four months, and that correlates directly with the periods when the batch pipeline and interactive traffic collide. If we cared only about latency, more hardware would be the fastest fix. It would also be the most expensive one, because the collision happens maybe fifteen hours a week, and we'd be paying depreciation on machines that exist to solve a scheduling conflict.

That points toward the middle path, which is where I think the actual answer lives. Before buying anything, we should spend six to eight weeks doing three things: partitioning the cluster so batch jobs can't starve the inference endpoint, moving our nightly training runs into the low-traffic window where the hardware is genuinely idle, and putting a real queueing layer in front of the whole thing so that utilisation becomes visible and accountable rather than anecdotal. None of this is glamorous. All of it is cheap relative to $180K, and — critically — all of it is reversible. If we restructure the scheduler and it turns out we were wrong about the headroom, we've lost a quarter of engineering time and learned something precise about our true ceiling. If we buy two nodes and we were wrong, we've lost capital, rack space, power budget, and we've locked in an operating cost that will follow us for three years. Asymmetry matters in decisions like this, and the asymmetry here does not favour purchasing.

There's also the opportunity cost to weigh honestly. The engineers who would integrate and validate new hardware are the same people who would build the scheduler improvements. Buying hardware doesn't create engineering capacity; it consumes it. The six weeks we'd spend racking, benchmarking, and migrating workloads onto new nodes is six weeks not spent on the inference caching work that our latency dashboard says would deliver a bigger improvement than either capacity option. Reliability cuts the same way: our two most recent outages were both caused by configuration drift during manual failovers, not by insufficient capacity. More machines means more failover paths, more drift surface, and more of exactly the kind of complexity that produced those incidents.

So my recommendation is: do not buy this quarter. Fund the utilisation work explicitly — I'd like us to treat it as a real project with a named owner, not a background chore — and set a decision gate at the end of it. If, after the scheduler work lands, our peak utilisation exceeds 80% and p99 latency still breaches our 500ms target, then we buy, and we buy with evidence rather than anxiety. I'd expect that gate to trigger, honestly, because our growth curve is real and the fleet is finite. But the order of operations matters. Buying first would mean paying for capacity we already own and never found.

One caveat I want on the record: my utilisation figures come from our monitoring stack, which we all know has gaps — the batch cluster reports occupancy, not useful work, and some of that 34% may be jobs that accomplish nothing. If the true number is even lower, the case for the utilisation path strengthens. If someone finds evidence that the fleet is actually saturated in ways our dashboards miss, I want to hear it before we commit either way. This is a recommendation, not a verdict, and it's falsifiable by design.

Happy to argue about it in Friday's session. Bring data.

— J.
